description: Barbarossa, Stalingrad, the Holocaust and total defeat — how the Second World War ended Nazi Germany.
content_html:
Germany at War 1939–1945

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. For the first two years the German military performed with devastating effectiveness, overrunning Poland, Denmark, Norway, France, the Low Countries and Yugoslavia in rapid succession. But the initial popular reaction to war in Germany was notably different from August 1914: there was no jubilation, only subdued acceptance. Germans had lived through one catastrophic war and feared another.

Changing Fortunes: Blitzkrieg to Barbarossa

The early victories generated genuine pride and consolidated Hitler’s authority. But the decision to invade the Soviet Union changed everything. Operation Barbarossa was launched on 22 June 1941, opening a front of extraordinary scale and brutality. Initial advances covered hundreds of miles, and German troops reached the outskirts of Moscow. But Soviet resistance stiffened, supply lines over-extended, and the Russian winter halted the advance.

The turning point came at Stalingrad. A German army besieging the city on the Volga was encircled by a Soviet counterattack in November 1942. After months of catastrophic urban fighting, Field Marshal Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943 with approximately 91,000 surviving troops (from an original force of over 300,000). It was the worst German military defeat of the war and the moment at which the tide irreversibly turned. After Stalingrad, the German army retreated continuously until May 1945.

Key Fact

The Wannsee Conference took place on 20 January 1942, chaired by Reinhard Heydrich. Senior Nazi officials coordinated the implementation of the “Final Solution” — the systematic murder of Europe’s Jewish population. Six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM).

The Holocaust

The Holocaust was the systematic, state-organised murder of approximately six million Jewish people — two-thirds of European Jewry. This figure, established by the USHMM and confirmed by Yad Vashem and the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, is the scholarly consensus. The murder was carried out in multiple ways: Einsatzgruppen (mobile killing units) shot an estimated 1.5 to 2 million Jews in mass executions across the occupied Soviet Union in 1941–42; and the death camps of occupied Poland — Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek — used gas chambers to murder hundreds of thousands at a time.

The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942, chaired by Reinhard Heydrich with Adolf Eichmann as secretary, co-ordinated the “Final Solution to the Jewish Question.” The conference minutes (the Wannsee Protocol) document the involvement of multiple Reich ministries, demonstrating that the Holocaust was not the work of a small group but required the participation of large parts of the German state apparatus.

Resistance intensified as the war turned against Germany. The White Rose was a student resistance group at Munich University. Between 1942 and early 1943, Hans and Sophie Scholl and their associates distributed leaflets denouncing Nazi crimes and calling for resistance. In February 1943, following Stalingrad, they scattered leaflets inside the university. A caretaker reported them to the Gestapo; Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested, tried by the People’s Court, and executed on 22 February 1943 — just days after their arrest.

The July Plot of 20 July 1944 was the most serious attempt to kill Hitler. Claus von Stauffenberg placed a briefcase bomb under a table in Hitler’s Wolf’s Lair headquarters. The bomb exploded, killing four people, but Hitler survived with minor injuries. The conspirators had hoped a successful assassination would enable a negotiated peace; instead, the Gestapo launched a massive purge. Approximately 5,000 people were subsequently arrested and around 200 executed, including von Stauffenberg himself (shot the same night) and many senior officers.

The Home Front and the Bombing of German Cities

The war had a profound impact on German civilians. Allied strategic bombing intensified from 1942, targeting industrial cities, ports and, controversially, city centres. The bombing of Dresden on 13–15 February 1945 killed approximately 22,700 to 25,000 civilians according to a 2010 historical commission — a figure lower than early Allied claims of 35,000 but higher than some post-war revisionist estimates. Dresden had genuine military significance as a transport hub, though the ethics of the raid remain debated.

By 1944 Nazi Germany was experiencing severe food shortages, labour shortages (addressed partly by the use of millions of forced labourers and concentration camp prisoners), and a steady deterioration of civilian morale. SD reports documented widespread private defeatism even among people who dared not express it openly. The regime responded with intensified terror: death sentences for “defeatism” became common.

Key Fact

Three wartime resisters: Hans and Sophie Scholl (White Rose, executed 22 Feb 1943 after distributing anti-Nazi leaflets); Claus von Stauffenberg (July Plot bomb attack 20 Jul 1944, executed same night); Dietrich Bonhoeffer (anti-Nazi theologian, executed Flossenbürg 9 Apr 1945).

By April 1945 Soviet forces had encircled Berlin. Hitler, in his underground bunker, refused to surrender and ordered the defence of the capital to the last. On 30 April 1945 he took his own life. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945 — Stunde Null (Zero Hour) in German historical memory. The country was in ruins: bombed, divided into four Allied occupation zones, its infrastructure shattered, millions of its people displaced.

The scale of destruction is difficult to comprehend. Approximately 6 million Jewish people had been murdered. An estimated 220,000 to 500,000 Roma had been killed (USHMM). Around 3 million Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity. Germany itself lost approximately 5 to 7 million military and civilian dead. The regime built on racial ideology had ended by destroying the nation it claimed to serve.
exam_tip_html: Holocaust questions require documentary precision: use the six million figure for Jewish victims (USHMM/Yad Vashem consensus), name specific mechanisms (Einsatzgruppen shootings in the East, death camps including Auschwitz-Birkenau), and date the Wannsee Conference accurately (20 January 1942). For questions on wartime resistance, distinguish clearly between different groups — the White Rose (students, leaflets, executed 1943), the July Plot (military officers, assassination attempt, 1944) and the Edelweiss Pirates (working-class youth, low-level defiance). Examiners’ reports note students confuse these groups — precise names, dates and actions separate strong answers from weak ones.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Operation Barbarossa (June 1941) opened the Eastern Front; the Stalingrad surrender (February 1943) marked the irreversible military turning point after which Germany retreated continuously.
  • The Holocaust murdered approximately six million Jewish people (USHMM); the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942) co-ordinated the “Final Solution,” involving multiple Reich ministries and demonstrating state-wide complicity.
  • Wartime resistance was real but small: the White Rose (executed February 1943) and July Plot (failed, July 1944) showed both the courage of resisters and the regime’s capacity for violent suppression.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, the conference co-ordinated the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question' — the systematic murder of Europe's Jewish population — with participation from multiple Reich ministries). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the White Rose resistance movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. led by students at Munich University including Hans and Sophie Scholl, who distributed anti-Nazi leaflets; Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested, tried by the People's Court and executed on 22 February 1943). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without sufficient detail. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Stalingrad (1942–43) was a turning point in Germany's experience of the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses military significance (encirclement of 300,000+ German troops, surrender of ~91,000), impact on civilian morale (SD reports of defeatism), change in military fortunes (Germany retreating from 1943), political impact (Hitler's authority questioned by elites). Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which opposition to the Nazi regime developed during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed forms of resistance with precise evidence (e.g. White Rose — students, leaflets, executed February 1943 after Stalingrad; July Plot — von Stauffenberg's bomb attack 20 July 1944, failed, mass purge followed). Analysis explains why wartime resistance developed. Secure: Two forms with relevant evidence. Developing: Two forms with limited analysis. Emerging: One form or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the impact of Allied bombing on the German war effort and civilian morale in the years 1942–1945?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the impact of bombing (Dresden, industrial targets, civilian casualties, SD morale reports) against other factors affecting the war effort (Eastern Front defeats, food and labour shortages, growing resistance). Uses Dresden figures precisely (22,700–25,000 — 2010 historical commission). Secure: Considers bombing's impact and compares with other factors with evidence. Developing: Describes bombing without comparative analysis. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that the Holocaust was the result of a long-term Nazi plan rather than wartime circumstances and escalation. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Engages with intentionalist vs functionalist historiographical debate without naming it as such: considers evidence of long-term intent (Mein Kampf, Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht) against evidence of wartime escalation (Einsatzgruppen 1941, Wannsee 1942 coordination, role of conquest of Soviet Union). Treats Holocaust with documentary specificity — six million figure, named methods, named events. Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both positions addressed with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: When did Germany surrender in the Second World War?
Hans and Sophie Scholl of the White Rose resistance movement were executed in which year?
Operation _____ was Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union, launched on 22 June 1941.
The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942 was chaired by Reinhard _____, who co-ordinated the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question.'
Match each act of resistance to the person(s) responsible:
right: Hans and Sophie Scholl — executed 22 February 1943

flashcard_questions.a: 22 June 1941 — Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened at Stalingrad in February 1943?
flashcard_questions.a: German Field Marshal Paulus surrendered ~91,000 surviving troops — the war's irreversible turning point.
Meeting of 20 January 1942 co-ordinating the 'Final Solution' — systematic murder of European Jews, chaired by Heydrich.

flashcard_questions.q: How many Jewish people were killed in the Holocaust?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately six million — two-thirds of European Jewry (USHMM/Yad Vashem consensus).
Mobile SS killing units that shot an estimated 1.5–2 million Jews in the occupied Soviet Union, 1941–42.

flashcard_questions.q: Who were Hans and Sophie Scholl?
flashcard_questions.a: Munich University students who led the White Rose resistance, distributing anti-Nazi leaflets; executed 22 February 1943.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened in the July Plot (20 July 1944)?
flashcard_questions.a: Von Stauffenberg's bomb exploded at Hitler's HQ but Hitler survived; around 200 conspirators were executed.

flashcard_questions.q: Death toll in the Dresden bombing?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 22,700 to 25,000 civilians (2010 historical commission estimate).

flashcard_questions.q: When did Hitler die, and how?
flashcard_questions.a: 30 April 1945 — suicide in his Berlin bunker as Soviet forces encircled the city.

glossary_terms.definition: Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union, launched on 22 June 1941 — the largest military operation in history, initially successful but ultimately leading to catastrophic German defeat.
Mobile killing units of the SS that followed the German army into the Soviet Union from June 1941, shooting an estimated 1.5 to 2 million Jews and other victims in mass executions.

Network of Nazi camps dedicated to the systematic murder of Jews and others, including Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek, where victims were killed primarily in gas chambers.
Conference held at Wannsee, Berlin, on 20 January 1942, at which senior Nazi officials co-ordinated the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question' — the systematic murder of all European Jews.

A student resistance group at Munich University, active 1942–1943, led by siblings Hans and Sophie Scholl, who distributed leaflets denouncing the Nazi regime. Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed on 22 February 1943.
German army officer who placed a bomb in a briefing room at Hitler's Wolf's Lair headquarters on 20 July 1944. The bomb exploded but Hitler survived; von Stauffenberg was executed the same night.
